listenings.text: Izabel, it is Sofia. The board pack closes on Friday at noon, so this is the last window for changes to your letter. Three things you asked me to confirm before you send it. First, the numbers. The delay in disclosure was three weeks, not two; I went back to the warehouse log and the first warning is dated the eighth. Second, the cadence. The weekly report has now run for thirty-one consecutive Thursdays without a single miss, which is the line I would put in bold, because it is the one thing nobody can argue with. Third, the oversight. Legal is comfortable with the wording as long as you say the report moves to operations in January, and not that it has already moved, because it has not. One personal note, if you will allow it. I have read the whole letter twice and the paragraph on candor is the best thing in it. Do not let anyone shorten that one to make room for the charts.

Izabel, David Chen. Something happened this week that I thought you should hear from me rather than from your sales team. Our board asked purchasing for an example of a supplier report worth copying, and I gave them yours. Not the case study, the one-page summary. What convinced them was not the recovery; it was that the failure and the fix sit on the same page, in the same size of type. My chairman called it the first supplier document he had read in five years that did not need a translator. So expect a call from our procurement group, and expect them to ask for the template. My advice, and you may ignore it: do not give them a template. Give them the rule behind it. A template can be filled in badly by anyone, and the rigor is not in the format, it is in the habit of publishing the number before somebody asks you for it.

reading.rtitle: The Year in One Page -- Letter to the Board
paras: To the board, from the CEO. What follows is the year in one page. The failure of the Halo sensor in the fourth quarter cost us two accounts and, for eleven weeks, the confidence of our largest client. Our first mistake was not the defect itself but the delay in disclosure: three weeks passed between the first warning from the warehouse and our decision to publish. Had the weekly report existed then, the fallout would have been smaller. It did not exist, and the loss of Meridian's trust was the price of that absence.

The recovery rested on three decisions. The first was the appointment of an external firm, which rebuilt the firmware we had failed to test properly. The second was the introduction of a weekly cadence: one report, every Thursday, with the numbers that flattered us next to the numbers that did not. The third, and the hardest, was the acceptance of scrutiny -- we sent the client the whole file rather than a summary. Not only did adoption climb from thirty-one to ninety-four percent; attrition fell to zero, and the renewal of the contract in May required no negotiation at all.

Two things follow from this year, and I ask the board to treat both as precedent. The first is a matter of governance: the weekly report is no longer a recovery measure but a permanent safeguard, and oversight of it moves to operations in January rather than staying with me. The second is a matter of stewardship. This company is not ours to gamble with, and candor is expensive in the first quarter and cheap in every quarter after it. The publication of our own bad numbers is what made the good ones believable, and the rigor of that report is what will keep them honest. The groundwork is done. What remains is the discipline to keep it, and that is the mandate I am asking you to renew.
reading.source: AVRT -- annual letter to the board, drafted by the CEO

gapfill.text: Nominalization turns a verb into a noun so that the FACT can sit in the subject and be judged: we delayed the disclosure becomes the delay in disclosure cost us three weeks. Watch the three patterns: decide becomes the decision TO publish, delay becomes the delay IN disclosure, lose becomes the loss OF their trust. The preposition is not decoration -- it changes with the noun, and it is never optional.

bank.label: Useful language for the one-page summary
items: The decision to publish the numbers was mine.
The delay in disclosure cost us three weeks.
The loss of their trust was the price of that delay.
The introduction of a weekly cadence changed the account.
The acceptance of scrutiny is what made us credible.
The renewal of the contract required no negotiation.

lf.text: TO carries an action you chose: the decision to publish, the refusal to argue. IN carries the thing that went wrong inside a process: the delay in disclosure, the drop in adoption. OF is the default and links the noun to what it acts on: the loss of their trust, the publication of the numbers. When in doubt, of is the safe one -- but never leave the preposition out.

items: Say what the three-week wait cost the company, starting the sentence with the noun: the delay...
Say who made the choice to publish, starting with the noun: the decision...
Say what the weekly report did to the account, starting with the noun: the introduction...
Summarize the whole year in four sentences, and open at least three of them with a noun phrase instead of a verb.

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
list: Gap-fill: 1 = delay, 2 = loss, 3 = decision, 4 = acceptance, 5 = renewal.
Scenario 1: 'The delay in disclosure cost us three weeks and two accounts.'
Scenario 2: 'The decision to publish the numbers was mine.'
Scenario 3: 'The introduction of a weekly cadence turned the account around.'
answerkey.note: TO for a chosen action, IN for what went wrong inside a process, OF for everything else. Never drop the preposition.
